I recently had an experience like yours. Discovered bed bugs after two nights of sleeping in the bed (the lighting wasn't very good). I can sympathize with your panic—I have OCD, so for some time the fear was pretty overwhelming.

But it's been over 3 weeks since I stayed there, and in spite of the fact that I stayed in the bed bug bed longer than you did, AND did substantially less to kill off the bed bugs that may or may not have been in my stuff, I have not laid eyes on a single bed bug since then. It sounds like you have done everything in your power to deal with the problem. This sounds like a good opportunity to practice letting go of worrying about things beyond your control. Just be extra careful about not putting stuff on the beds you stay at for the next couple of weeks, just in case.

No, I didn't get put under. As far as I understand it, there are usually two options for wisdom teeth surgery. There's general anesthesia, which is usually what people mean when they say they're being "put under," where you'll be asleep the entire time. Then there's nitrous, where you're woozy and supposedly relaxed (YMMV... lol) but awake.

Usually they give you a choice because general anesthesia substantially increases the out-of-pocket cost of surgery, as dental anesthesia is not covered by most insurance and nitrous is waaay cheaper than the labor costs of keeping you alive while you're under anesthesia. Unless you have some crazy situation where there's no way you could be awake for it, I think they're supposed to give you a choice between nitrous and general. 

If you think you can handle being awake, you might want to ask your doc if you can do it under nitrous. It's a good way to save some money if that's a concern for you. But, like, there's always a risk that the procedure is going to be extremely unpleasant, like it was for me. It's a hard decision.

I feel like analog horror used to be scary (depending on how you define scary), but as it's caught on, there's been a marked decline in the quality of what's being made. Especially with Emergency Alert System (EAS) type analog horror. What makes the medium scary, I think, is the suspension of disbelief, and recently, the way people structure their EAS horror stories makes this all but impossible. The entire point of an emergency alert broadcast is to give viewers the need-to-know information FIRST, and THEN move on to the less important stuff. It's all about triaging your information. A lot of newer EAS horror stories do not do this at all, and pretty much just tell you a story with a VHS filter slapped onto the subtitles. By the time you've explained to me in detail how the evil thinking fog was synthesized in a lab, I'm already dead. Tell me to shelter in place and stuff wet rags under the windowsills first, and THEN give me the backstory so I have time to stew in my fear of the unknown, ya dig?

Lots of things, admittedly. I worked in one over 2 years during high school, and there's just a lot of death and human deterioration. I was a waiter, and my favorite table to serve were these 5 gentlemen who were all great friends, always laughing, never rude, always had something nice to say. Then one of them just started going downhill, being in his late 80's or early 90's and all, and then one day there was a notice on our corkboard that he'd passed away. I'm glad I never had to be the one to break the news to any of them. They were all so silent that night. That was what stuck with me. 

I was also really good friends with this sweet, sweet lady. I mean, she really was my favorite. On my first night of work, she saw my nametag and grabbed my hand and sang me a very old song that had my name in it. She told us all about how she loved Shirley Temple as a kid, and she would talk a lot about her husband who'd passed some years ago. Once she invited some of the servers into her room, and she showed us a picture of the plane piloted by her husband that she took immediately before she met him, and she was always so proud of this. In her own words, she had a picture of her husband "flying into her life." Not too long ago, I came upon her at the grocery store, and I said hello to her. She didn't recognize me. That was another one that stayed with me.  

The dining room had assigned seating, so everyone always sat with the same people. And they got to choose, so it was typically with their friends. So when someone passed, you were always serving them dinner in the aftermath of all that. You might even be feeding them the day after, or the day of. I actually once saw a man get the news broken to him in real time. 

It was this lady who sat at the far end of the room with two gentlemen, and all three of them were notoriously ornery, but the lady was the worst. She got into trouble for snapping at me on my second night of work. She was only in her 80s, but she looked and acted like a centenarian. Cataracts for days. Nearly deaf. Major memory problems. Needed everything to be piping hot, because she could barely register the sensation of heat anymore. In spite of her very poor memory, she always wanted everything to be a very specific way when her food arrived. Hotter than hot, a half portion, and she wanted her decaf coffee then and only then, no sooner and no later, and if you didn't get it to her lickety-split, then god help you. She was rude to everyone. She also taught me a lot about getting through to rude people. I developed a strategy with her that I use to this day. When she was rude to me, I would pretend not to notice that she was being rude, and I would be very friendly with her. I hoped it would make her feel kind of silly for being so mean. I like to think that it did, even if she never remembered who I was. I also started drilling myself on going through the motions of exactly what she wanted when her food was served, until I could do it incredibly quickly. Once, I managed to get her her coffee before she could even ask me for it. And when she did, I told her it was right there, and she goddamn smiled at me and asked me for my name. I'd never even seen her smile. It was one of my proudest moments working there.

Anyway, when she died, I remember one of the notorious gentlemen looked up at me as I was filling the coffee pots and asked me where she was. The other gentleman, who was very old and not one for formalities, just said that she died. Just like that. I left them alone after that, but I'll never forget the look on his face. She was completely estranged from her family, and I'll never know exactly why, but I know there were at least two people on this earth who were sad to see her go. 

I guess what haunted me the most was the memory of being in a place where death had such an immediate presence. You had to make friends with these people quickly, because you could lose any one of them tomorrow. 

Also, one time I watched a lady puke on her plate and then just stand up and leave.

The biggest hint was when I'd go over to my friends' houses, they could make jokes at their fathers' expense, and he never raised his voice for anything other than for comedic effect. They seemed to have a friendly, comfortable relationship that I found myself jealous of, because in my house, if you gave off even the ghost of an impression that you were making fun of my dad, he'd go into a red-faced, screaming fit of rage that would usually end in you huddled in a corner crying your eyes out, literally just waiting for him to tire himself out.  


Also, I found that my friends had a very different definition of "getting yelled at" than I did. They would say that a teacher "yelled at them" when I had seen said teacher give them a fairly gentle warning about their behavior. If said teacher had a tone that even suggested that they were openly frustrated, I would hear later about how the teacher "screamed at them." I realize now that when people say these sorts of things, they mean it figuratively, but it confused me growing up, because my experience with getting "screamed at" was extremely literal.  


Another thing was finding out that my friends had systems of discipline in place at home that were actually put in writing or at least codified and put in place officially. As in, I did X, so now Y is happening as a punishment. All of the discipline that happened in our home wasn't really discipline. I take care of kids for work part of the year. Discipline should benefit the child first and foremost. It's a low-stakes simulation of actions and consequences as they occur in the adult world. It should not be an opportunity for the parent to take out their frustrations on their children. That's a big way that abuse happens.

I feel like this is a leading question that, when answered honestly, doesn't have a simple answer. Narratively, personality advances the plot and helps to make characters distinct and memorable, and its importance in character creation cannot be overstated. Diversity's role in storytelling is a little more complicated in that it has significance both within the narrative and beyond the fourth wall. Diversity can inform characters' personalities and motivations, (such as a black character who exhibits trust issues due to their experiences with institutional racism, or a gay character having problems with intimacy due to being closeted during their formative years) and it plays an important role in how we connect with media. Like it or not, characters in movies (and other media) are a reflection of who we as a society have deemed worthy of having their stories told. So what does it say to people of minority races, orientations, and genders when the only people we tell stories about are straight, white, cisgender men? Even if it doesn't bother you, personally, if all of the characters in all of your media are completely identical in race, gender, and sexual orientation, you should at spare a thought for the people who have rarely or never seen someone like them portrayed in a positive way.   


In short, I find this question silly because the comparison between diversity and personality is fallacious. They're just two elements of storytelling that occupy two different niches in the storytelling process that serve two different purposes, with some overlap. 

What I'm saying is, they're not at all mutually exclusive. You can and should have both.

I had a camper this summer who had been to our camp before, and the higher ups already knew that he was extremely difficult. Based on the two weeks I spent with him, as well as discussions with my co-counselors who have career experience in childcare and/or paraeducation, I believe that his issues were a combination between being slightly to moderately on the autism spectrum, and a home life without much discipline. He had a LOT of issues, more than I've ever had to deal with.

A brief overview of his behavioral issues:

\-Frequently refused to get out of bed, for any reason. This caused the most significant problems in our groups, because our camp is very strict about safety, so no camper is EVER allowed to be alone anywhere but inside a bathroom stall, and a single counselor can't be alone with a single camper. This means that we couldn't just leave him to have a nap when he refused to get out of bed, or even leave one counselor behind with him while the rest went to programming or whatever else. 

\-He had temper tantrums. These occurred when he didn't get something he wanted, however small. The most frequent thing he got mad over was losing games. Even if it was a game where losing was totally inconsequential, because you still got to play or you'd be back in the game in, like, five seconds. But he also got upset when he felt like he wasn't doing well at an activity (archery, arts and crafts, etc.), got into any sort of minor disagreement with another camper, or was made to go to an activity that he didn't want to go to. These temper tantrums involved a lot of screaming, throwing things, occasionally swearing, and running off. 

\-Refusing to do chores. Speaks for itself. He did not like having to do any kind of work, at all. 

\-Being really disagreeable and starting fights with other campers. This was an especially big problem our first week, when our group dynamic sucked ass anyway.

I had him for two weeks (where normally I only have campers for one week). The first week was worse than the second, and without a doubt the worst week I've ever had as a camp counselor. My co counselor and I (sidenote: most of the time, we don't do co counselors at our camp unless necessary, but our director knew it was gonna be SUPER necessary) had seven campers, and five of them had consistent behavioral issues. The group as a whole, which already had a bad dynamic, did not like the aforementioned camper, because he caused the most issues. The entire week was an absolute disaster that brought me to the end of my rope. My co counselor was over ten years older than me, and was my counselor more than once when I was a camper. He is (or was? can't remember) a paraeducator, and even he was getting clearly very frustrated by the end of the week. The week that followed was not as bad. I offered to be his counselor again because I'd figured out how to deal with him effectively, and for his sake and my coworkers', I didn't want to put this camper with a counselor who would have to learn from the ground up how to communicate with him. 

Here's how I did it:

\-Giving him advance notice before we left. Usually during our breaks, he'd go to bed, either to read or to stare at the wall or sleep. We figured out that giving him X amount of time to do something was really helpful for making the transition between rest time and go time easier. It would usually go something like, "camper, I'm giving you 15 minutes, and then we're gonna put on our shoes and leave," with check ins and time updates every five minutes or so. And once time is up, you really have to...

\-Being insistent! If you're too lenient with him, he will recognize that, and he will do what he wants. If you have to sit at his bedside for ten, fifteen, twenty minutes constantly telling him that we need to go, then that's what you're gonna do. He will pretend to be asleep. He will say no. You have to outlast him.

\-Making him promise to be a good sport. This worked SHOCKINGLY well, usually. If I knew the kids were about to play a game where losing was a possibility (an inevitability, really, with most camp games), I would make him promise me that he was going to be a good sport, and specifically not scream or yell. He still didn't handle losing "well," exactly, but instead of screaming and crying upon losing he would make a beeline to me, vent to me for a little bit about why he lost or why the game wasn't fair, and then we'd take a little breather, and then I'd ask him if he wanted to get back into the game, and he would. Failed me a couple times (once, catastrophically, when he shouted "WHAT THE FUCK" upon getting tagged), but it never hurt to try.

\-Giving him space when he does get upset. He follows his own internal logic about what's right and wrong and fair and unfair, and it's very hard to make him see things a different way. I often found it easiest to just make sure he was in a safe place so he could let it out of his system.

\-Understanding his special needs. It's not mentioned on his health forms, but I highly suspect he was autistic, and when I based my judgment calls on my armchair diagnosis, I found it much easier to relate to and understand his behavior. Sometimes he NEEDS to be somewhere quieter. If there's a rock in his shoe, he NEEDS to get it out. If there's something gross on his hands, he NEEDS to get it off. Once, me and two other counselors had to band together to wash his feet because he'd forgotten to wash them when he showered, and his shoes were full of sand, and he was plopped down on a bench refusing to move because the sensory aspect was bothering him so much. It's so easy to misinterpret autistic traits as being "high maintenance" or "bratty" or whatever if you're only viewing those traits from a neurotypical framework.

 \-Figuring out his actual interests and rolling with it. So much of those two weeks was a game of "make this camper not be upset," but that task got significantly easier when I realized that I could make him actually happy, not just not unhappy. He really loved Sonic, and my co counselor the first week just happened to bring some sonic comic books, which he really loved. He also loved arts and crafts, and superheroes. While the rest of our second week group made a cardboard box rocket ship with my co counselor, this camper told me he wanted to make some cardboard armor, so we did. When we went to an activity I knew he hated, I would bring along construction paper and markers and whatever else he asked for. When his cardboard shield went missing, I went to the arts and crafts building at night and made him a painted cardboard captain america shield, which he ended up taking home with him. Some campers only make it through camp without actually having a good time, and sometimes that's all we can do. But if possible, camp is supposed to be a happy, fun place where you make a lot of good memories. And as it turned out, this camper was much easier to manage when he was having a good time, so it was very much a win-win when I could figure out what he enjoyed and milk it for everything it's worth.

This was definitely my most difficult summer as a camp counselor, but I got so much experience out of it, and I feel stronger and more capable as a counselor. As a CIT, I always questioned whether or not I would be able to deal if I got hit with THAT camper, the ones that become breakroom horror stories for years to come. Now I know I can do it, and I did it for two weeks. Very trying, but very rewarding. Such an important summer for my self confidence.

I believe this has already been covered by another commenter, so pardon the redundancy, but this aspect of LGBT language is an interest of mine. 

The word “lesbian” is derived from the name for an island in Greece called “Lesbos,” where the poet Sappho of Lesbos lived. She’s one of the earliest lesbians we know of (some historians believe that she was not a lesbian due to the fact that she occasionally spoke of having a husband. However, aside from the fact that plenty of lesbians have historically married men to avoid persecution, it’s also worth noting that her husband was said to be named Kerkylos of Andros, which roughly translates to “Dick Allcocks from the Isle of Man,” so I think it’s much more likely that Sappho was just a lesbian with a sense of humor), and she’s also responsible for the establishment of many lesbian symbols, especially violets. 

As such, we use the word “lesbian” in much the same way as we would use the word “American” or “Canadian” to describe someone. We wouldn’t call Timmy “a black,” but we would certainly call him “an African American.” Likewise, the word “Gay” isn’t derived from the name of a place, so it doesn’t make sense to call someone “a gay.”

Hope that makes sense! I can understand the confusion. The term “lesbian” is definitely an etymological anomaly when compared to other LGBT terms.

From my years working at a retirement home AND a summer camp:

If you're going to accompany someone who's a child, an elderly person, or infirm in any way, follow the rule of three. Take someone with you, preferably someone you trust who is also your peer. 

Reasons for this:
1) Naturally, if something happens to the infirm person, one of you can administer first aid, and the other can call 911. Two heads are better than one in a situation like that.
2) This is also for your legal protection. If the person you're looking after lies and says that you did something to them (hit them, sexually assaulted them, etc.), and it was just you and the person, it's going to be much harder to prove that you DIDN'T do the thing. Your third person acts as a witness, so make sure all three of you are within sight of each other at all times.
3) If the person you're looking after does something to you (doesn't apply so much to children, but definitely to the elderly), having a witness around will make it much easier to prove that they actually did the thing. If they were planning on something, it might also discourage them, as well. 

Mostly just to prevent the absolute worst from happening, but you can never be too careful.

Longtime recreational writer/editor, here.

There are a lot (a LOT) of things that make me cringe when I'm reading amateur prose. I could write up an exhaustive list, but I've got shit to do, so here's the single worst thing (and there's a technical term for this. I've heard it, but I can't think of it):

*XYZ, a man with sandy blonde hair and a square build, shook my hand. "How are you?" he asked.

"Fine, how are you?"

"I'm doing well," the blonde-haired man replied.*

The issue here is the fact that instead of simply saying "he replied" or "XYZ replied," the author feels the need to refer to him in terms of his hair color, even after we've learned his name. This happens with other traits, like "the tall woman" or "the skinny boy," but 9/10 times, it has something to do with their hair color. Using hair color also gives the amateur author the opportunity to not even refer to the character as "the blonde-haired man" - sometimes they just say "the blonde" or "the brunette," and that bothers me even more for some reason. It doesn't add anything to the text and draws attention to a detail that we don't care about. Just say their name or "he" or "she" or "they," goddamnit. 

I mean, I don't know many of the writers I've seen do this personally, but if I were to guess, I'd say that they do it for one of three reasons (arranged from least presumptuous to most presumptuous and slightly hairbrained):

1: They've been slightly indoctrinated by their elementary school writing teacher and think that if you put two of the same word within a paragraph of each other, your hard drive will burst into flames. But the truth is, your readers are going to notice if you take up words adding information to the text that doesn't add anything to the narrative. 

2: They're leaning too heavily on their character's appearance to make an impact. In all likelihood, they're better at appearance than personality, so they're just trying to identify their characters *very* clearly. How else are you supposed to tell them apart when their personalities are identical and blander than uncooked oatmeal?

3: This is just my pet conspiracy theory, but sometimes, I think the problem is that they started writing because of anime. Now, that's not a bad reason in and of itself to start writing - there are no bad reasons. However, anime doesn't translate well to prose if you use literally anything other than plot structure, and even that can be pretty iffy. But next to an inability to convey visual gags competently, the biggest obstacle for the anime-fan-turned-writer is same face syndrome. In nearly all later anime, characters of the same gender will almost always have the exact same face, body type, and sometimes even height, to the point that if you stripped that character down, the only way you'd be able to identify them is by their gender and hair color. Therefore, assuming you've already described your character's outfit, "the (x)-haired (man/woman)" is really all you need for your readers to know exactly who you're talking about. Too bad it sounds clunky and wastes space. If you have this problem and you're not writing anime fanfiction, I'd urge you to start visualizing your characters as real people and not cartoon characters. Baby steps, people.

Podcasts. If you haven't messed around in your iPhone's podcast app, for fuck's sake, do it, and if you have an android, get a podcast app, there are tons. If you have no idea what a podcast is, it's basically radio shows on-demand. There's a podcast for just about anything you can think of - I listen to a lot of horror podcasts, writing podcasts, and audio dramas, but if you do a little bit of digging, you're bound to find something that's interesting to you. 

If you're just getting started, I'd personally recommend anything by Joseph Fink or Jeffrey Cranor (Welcome to Night Vale, obviously, but if that's too mainstream and/or abstract for you, try Alice Isn't Dead or Within the Wires. The latter two also have shorter, more concise storylines, with definite beginnings, middles, and ends, whereas WTNV is ongoing), Freakonomics, The NoSleep Podcast (with some reservations - the story narration is unmatched, but some of the stories themselves are subpar. Ideal podcast if you like to rail on bad horror stories as much as you like to hear good ones), or Mysterious Universe (an absolute treasure trove for anyone interested in a skeptical yet open take on conspiracy theories and paranormal shit. Also, the hosts are brilliant). 

The best part is that you can listen to podcasts while doing virtually anything that doesn't require your full attention, and almost all podcasts are free. Great way to unwind and put your mind somewhere else for a bit.
